description: Revvity, Inc. provides health sciences solutions, technologies, and services. The company offers instruments, reagents, software, subscriptions, detection and imaging technologies, extended warranties
description_full: Revvity, Inc. provides health sciences solutions, technologies, and services. The company offers instruments, reagents, software, subscriptions, detection and imaging technologies, extended warranties, and training and services; and instruments, reagents, and assay platforms and software products for early detection of common and rare conditions, such as pregnancy and early childhood, as well as infectious disease testing in the diagnostics market. Its products are used for testing and screening genetic abnormalities, disorders, and diseases, including down syndrome, hypothyroidism, muscular dystrophy, infertility, and various metabolic conditions. It also develops technologies that enable and support genomic workflows using protein coupled receptors and next-generation DNA sequencing for oncology, immunodiagnostics, and drug discovery. It serves pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies, laboratories, academic and research institutions, public health authorities, private healthcare organizations, doctors, and government agencies under the AutoDELFIA, chemagic, Chitas, CNGnome, DELFIA, DELFIA Xpress, EONIS, EUROArray, EUROIMMUN, EUROLabWorkstation, EUROLINE, EUROPattern, Evolution Evoya, GSP, Haoyuan, IDS Immunodiagnosticsystems, IDS-i10, IDS-i10T, IDS-i20, IDS-iSYS, iLab, iQ, LifeCycle, LimsLink, Migele, NeoBase, NeoLSD, NEXTFLEX, Panthera Puncher, PreNAT II, Prime, RONIA, SimplicityChrom, Specimen Gate, Superflex, Symbio, T-SPOT, Vanadis, ViaCord, VICTOR2, and WholePanel brand names, as well as under the Accell, AlphaLISA, AlphaPlex, AlphaScreen, Alpha SureFire, AssayMate, BIOCHIPs, BioLegend, Bioo Scientific, BioQule, Brilliant Violet, Ce3D, CellCarrier, Cellaca, Celigo, Cellometer, cell::explorer, Cell-Vive, Chalice, ChemDraw, CHOSOURCE, Dharmacon, and DharmaFECT brand names. The company was formerly known as PerkinElmer, Inc. and changed its name to Revvity, Inc. in April 2023. Revvity, Inc. was founded in 1937 and is headquartered in Waltham, Massachusetts.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 11K people. Revenue per employee of $260K ranks in the below the sector median among Healthcare peers. Each employee generates $46K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $2K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 14× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (8/10).
financial_summary: Revvity, Inc. is a large-cap healthcare business with a $17.2B market cap on $2.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -5% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 3% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 48%.

The business throws off $509M in free cash flow — roughly 18 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.42× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.0× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 3.9×.

Shareholder yield of 5.0% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Goodwill represents 54% of total assets — a large impairment risk hanging over book value
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Carries a 41% premium to sector median EV/EBITDA (confirmed by 1 other valuation measure)
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Above-average short interest at 8.8% of float
Insiders are overwhelmingly selling (100% sell ratio) — the people who know the business want less of it
Revenue growth lags most Healthcare peers — losing share inside the profit pool
Patent cliffs, drug-pricing reform, and reimbursement pressure — a single regulatory change can reset the pricing power that justifies the multiple.
Clinical trial concentration risk — binary FDA outcomes on a lead asset can wipe out billions in market cap in a single session.
GLP-1 disruption across sub-sectors — weight-loss drugs are reshaping demand for orthopaedics, cardiovascular devices, and sleep-apnea treatments in ways not yet priced in.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 13% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
42 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Healthcare sector showing strong relative momentum, outperforming the market by 13% over 3 months
Healthcare ETF in a sustained uptrend above its long-term average

sect: Its 12% operating margin runs 13pp above the Healthcare median (0%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.43x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-23.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 462 companies in the universe; the top four hold 35% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 66% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 40% and a beta of 1.02, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $250.6M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 34% in the 2020 crash, 39% in the 2022 bear market and 63% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $127 (margin of safety -21%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 52%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $93.26 to $179 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Healthcare peers: P/E 68.6 vs 26.2, EV/EBITDA 21.8 vs 15.5 and P/FCF 33.8 vs 23.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 86% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 15 covering analysts target $171 on average, 11% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 3% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.9%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.55).
It runs a 48% gross margin and converts 18% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.42x.
ROE of 3% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 7.6% of revenue on R&D and 0.8% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.0x net debt to EBITDA ($919.9M of cash against $3.2B of debt), with interest covered 3.9x.
Goodwill makes up 54% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -4.8% over 3 years, -5.5% over 5 years and 3.1% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -9.0% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.2x depreciation (2.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 12, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $1.5M sold).
It returns 5.0% a year to shareholders (4.8% in buybacks and 0.2% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.4% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 42 consecutive years, raising it 1.0% a year over the last five.
people: With about 11,000 employees, each generates about $260K of revenue, 0.7x the Healthcare median, and revenue has grown 3.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $46K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.6M (14x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
